course.title: Full-Stack Web Application Development with JavaScript & Node.js — Initial cohort draft
course.shortDescription: Six guided classes covering full-stack architecture and javascript; node.js servers and express routes; database modelling and persistence; authentication and access control; react integration and scalable api responses; api tests, documentation and deployment.
course.description:
A guided course for learners who want to build and explain a working student-management application.

Outcomes

  1. Diagram the browser, API and database. Build a five-student dataset with map/filter/find operations. Describe how an invalid request differs from an empty successful result.
  2. Implement list, detail and create student endpoints against temporary in-memory data. Test invalid JSON, a missing ID and a valid create request. Explain why this storage is only a development exercise.
  3. Persist students in a database and implement adding and retrieving them. Define a unique student code and a course relationship. Demonstrate duplicate rejection, parameterized input and persistence after restart.
  4. Build a login and protected profile flow using a maintained authentication library. Demonstrate anonymous rejection, expired-token rejection and denial when one student requests another student’s record. Explain hashing and authorization separately.
  5. Connect a React student list and create form to the API. Add bounded pagination and failure recovery. Explain what would happen with 100,000 records and distinguish I/O concurrency from CPU-heavy processing.
  6. Write an endpoint test and its API contract. Produce a production runbook covering configuration, database migration, startup, HTTPS, logging and rollback. Use a local or isolated preview rather than publishing real student records.
course.duration: 6 classes · 18 live hours plus independent practice
course.requirements: Basic computer use, a code editor, a browser and a local development environment. Frontend framework tracks assume basic JavaScript; backend tracks include introductory language review.
course.targetAudience: Learners building their first structured web application; instructors should review prerequisites with the cohort.

class.title: 01. Full-stack architecture and JavaScript
class.objectives: Explain full-stack architecture and javascript; implement the demonstrated workflow; test a normal and a failure case; justify design choices using evidence.

sections.title: Introduction and context
sections.body: A student-management application spans a browser interface, a server and persistent storage. Trace one request through these boundaries before implementing the endpoints.

sections.title: Lesson plan · 180 minutes
sections.body: 15 min: recall and goals; 45 min: guided explanation; 30 min: code demonstration; 10 min: break; 45 min: practical exercise; 20 min: review and quiz; 15 min: assignment briefing.

sections.title: Concepts and explanations
sections.body: The browser submits an HTTP request; the server validates input and authorization, queries storage and returns an appropriate response. JavaScript arrays and objects represent records in memory but do not persist across restarts. Use map, filter and find for distinct data operations. An async function returns a promise, and await pauses that function until a promise settles without making slow CPU work non-blocking. Plan both success and failure responses.

sections.body:

console.log(students.filter(s => s.score >= 70).map(s => s.name)); // ['Ada']

questions.text: What is full-stack development?

options.text: Developing both frontend and backend parts of an application

questions.explanation: Full-stack development involves working across the frontend, backend, databases, APIs, and related application infrastructure.

questions.text: What is the primary purpose of a web API?

options.text: To allow software systems to communicate with each other

questions.explanation: APIs provide defined ways for different software systems to exchange data and functionality.

questions.text: Which HTTP method is commonly used to retrieve information?
questions.explanation: GET requests are generally used to retrieve resources.

questions.text: What does CRUD represent?
questions.explanation: CRUD represents the four fundamental operations commonly performed on application data.

questions.text: What is the purpose of a database in a web application?

options.text: To persist and organize application data

questions.explanation: Databases provide persistent storage and mechanisms for retrieving and managing application data.

questions.text: A React frontend needs to retrieve customer information from a Node.js backend. What would typically be used?

options.text: A database password exposed to the browser

questions.explanation: The frontend can communicate with the backend through defined API endpoints.

questions.text: Which keyword is commonly used to declare a variable that should not be reassigned?
questions.explanation: `const` creates a variable binding that cannot be reassigned.

questions.text: What is an arrow function?

options.text: A concise syntax for writing functions

questions.explanation: Arrow functions provide a shorter syntax for defining functions.

questions.text: What does the `map()` method do?

options.text: Creates a new array by transforming each element

questions.explanation: `map()` applies a function to every element and returns a new array containing the results.

questions.text: What does the `filter()` method do?

options.text: Returns elements that satisfy a condition

questions.explanation: `filter()` creates a new array containing elements for which the supplied condition returns true.

class.title: 02. Node.js servers and Express routes
class.objectives: Explain node.js servers and express routes; implement the demonstrated workflow; test a normal and a failure case; justify design choices using evidence.

sections.title: Introduction and context
sections.body: Node.js runs JavaScript outside the browser. Express supplies routing and middleware so requests can pass through shared checks before reaching a handler.

sections.title: Lesson plan · 180 minutes
sections.body: 15 min: recall and goals; 45 min: guided explanation; 30 min: code demonstration; 10 min: break; 45 min: practical exercise; 20 min: review and quiz; 15 min: assignment briefing.

sections.title: Concepts and explanations
sections.body: A route combines an HTTP method and path. Parse JSON bodies before routes that need them, validate every request and return a single response. Treat IDs from URLs as untrusted input. Return 404 for a missing student, 400 for invalid data and a suitable success status when a record is created. Middleware order matters: authentication must run before a protected handler. Use centralized error handling that avoids returning stack traces to clients.

sections.title: Worked demonstration
sections.body:
Read the example, predict its output or behavior, then run it in the appropriate project. Framework snippets assume the lesson project and the shown imports or surrounding setup. Inspect the result before making the extension below.

import express from 'express';
const app = express();
app.use(express.json());
app.get('/students', (req, res) => res.json([]));
app.get('/students/:id', (req, res) => res.status(404).json({message: 'Student not found'}));
app.listen(3000);

class.title: 03. Database modelling and persistence
class.objectives: Explain database modelling and persistence; implement the demonstrated workflow; test a normal and a failure case; justify design choices using evidence.

sections.title: Introduction and context
sections.body: Persistent records need identifiers, constraints and a clear relationship model. Choose storage based on the data and queries rather than treating a database as a larger array.

sections.title: Lesson plan · 180 minutes
sections.body: 15 min: recall and goals; 45 min: guided explanation; 30 min: code demonstration; 10 min: break; 45 min: practical exercise; 20 min: review and quiz; 15 min: assignment briefing.

sections.title: Concepts and explanations
sections.body: A relational design can separate students, courses and enrollments, using foreign keys to connect valid records. Unique constraints prevent duplicate identifiers even when requests arrive together. Parameterized queries separate data from SQL syntax. A transaction groups dependent changes so they either all succeed or all roll back. Use migrations to reproduce schema changes and test restart persistence. Indexes can speed targeted reads but have a write and storage cost.

questions.text: What is a primary key?

questions.text: What is a database index primarily used for?

options.text: Improving the efficiency of certain data retrieval operations

questions.text: An application frequently searches users by email address. What could improve query performance?

questions.text: Which test demonstrates persistent storage?

options.text: Create a record, restart the app, and retrieve it

questions.explanation: A process restart removes memory-only state while durable storage remains.

class.title: 04. Authentication and access control
class.objectives: Explain authentication and access control; implement the demonstrated workflow; test a normal and a failure case; justify design choices using evidence.

sections.title: Introduction and context
sections.body: Authentication establishes identity; authorization determines what that identity may do. An authenticated student must still be prevented from reading another student’s private submission.

sections.title: Lesson plan · 180 minutes
sections.body: 15 min: recall and goals; 45 min: guided explanation; 30 min: code demonstration; 10 min: break; 45 min: practical exercise; 20 min: review and quiz; 15 min: assignment briefing.

sections.title: Concepts and explanations
sections.body: Store password hashes using a maintained password-hashing implementation, never plaintext or reversible encryption. Verify tokens cryptographically and validate their expiry and expected claims. Derive identity from the verified session rather than a client-supplied student ID. Check resource ownership or role at every protected endpoint. Login errors should avoid exposing whether an account exists. Limit repeated attempts and keep credentials out of logs and source control.

sections.title: Worked demonstration
sections.body:
Read the example, predict its output or behavior, then run it in the appropriate project. Framework snippets assume the lesson project and the shown imports or surrounding setup. Inspect the result before making the extension below.

// After trusted authentication middleware sets req.user:
if (submission.studentId !== req.user.id && req.user.role !== 'ADMIN') {
  return res.status(403).json({message: 'Access denied'});
}
return res.json(submission);

options.text: Determining what a user is allowed to do

questions.explanation: Authentication verifies that a user is who they claim to be.

questions.text: What is authorization?

options.text: Determining what an authenticated user is permitted to access or perform

questions.explanation: Authorization determines what actions or resources an authenticated user can access.

questions.text: Why should passwords be hashed?

options.text: To make passwords easier to read
To allow administrators to retrieve passwords
To remove the need for authentication
To avoid storing the original password directly

questions.explanation: Password hashing helps protect user credentials if stored password data is compromised.

questions.text: What is JWT commonly used for?

options.text: Carrying signed claims for authentication or authorization

questions.explanation: JSON Web Tokens can carry signed claims and are commonly used in authentication systems.

questions.text: Why should sensitive secrets such as API keys not be committed to Git repositories?

options.text: They may be exposed to unauthorized users

questions.explanation: Public or improperly secured repositories can expose credentials. Secrets should be managed using environment variables or secret-management systems.

questions.text: A user has a valid login token but tries to access an administrator endpoint. What should happen?

options.text: The backend should verify the user's permissions before granting access
The token should automatically grant administrator access

questions.explanation: A valid authentication token proves identity or session validity, but authorization must still determine whether the user has the required permissions.

questions.text: A student changes a URL ID to another student’s submission. What should stop access?

options.text: A server-side ownership or permission check

questions.explanation: Authentication alone does not authorize every resource.

questions.text: What should be stored for password verification?

options.text: A hash from a maintained password-hashing implementation

questions.explanation: Password hashes support verification without storing recoverable plaintext.

questions.text: Where should an authenticated request obtain its trusted identity?

options.text: From the verified session or token

questions.explanation: Client-supplied ownership claims require verification and cannot establish identity.

questions.text: A signed token is past its expiry time. What should the API do?

options.text: Accept it forever because it is signed

questions.explanation: Token validation includes time constraints as well as signature verification.

sections.title: Introduction and context
sections.body: The browser needs an API contract that remains useful as data grows. Coordinate the UI states with pagination, errors and asynchronous work on the server.

sections.title: Lesson plan · 180 minutes
sections.body: 15 min: recall and goals; 45 min: guided explanation; 30 min: code demonstration; 10 min: break; 45 min: practical exercise; 20 min: review and quiz; 15 min: assignment briefing.

sections.title: Concepts and explanations
sections.body: A frontend request should check the response status before parsing a success payload. Show loading, empty and error states and preserve form data after rejection. Validate pagination limits on the backend; returning every record becomes expensive as a roster grows. Use stable ordering and document page semantics. Rate limiting controls repeated requests but does not replace authentication. CPU-heavy synchronous work can still block the Node event loop even when the containing function is async.

sections.title: Worked demonstration
sections.body:
Read the example, predict its output or behavior, then run it in the appropriate project. Framework snippets assume the lesson project and the shown imports or surrounding setup. Inspect the result before making the extension below.

const response = await fetch('/students?page=0&size=20');
if (!response.ok) throw new Error('Unable to load students');
const page = await response.json();
// Render page.items and use the API pagination metadata.

sections.title: Guided practical exercise
sections.body:
Connect a React student list and create form to the API. Add bounded pagination and failure recovery. Explain what would happen with 100,000 records and distinguish I/O concurrency from CPU-heavy processing.

Work in a disposable project using synthetic student data. Record expected behavior before running it. Compare the result with your prediction and explain one mistake you corrected.

sections.title: Key takeaways and self-check
sections.body: Explain the input, transformation and output of your solution. Identify one boundary where data can fail or access must be checked. Describe the evidence that your solution handles that boundary. Return to the concepts above if you cannot explain your code without reading it aloud.

questions.text: What is React primarily used for?
questions.explanation: React is a JavaScript library for building user interfaces using reusable components.

questions.text: What are props?

options.text: Data passed from a parent component to a child component

questions.explanation: Props allow components to receive data and configuration from their parent components.

questions.text: Which Hook is commonly used to manage local component state?
questions.explanation: `useState` allows functional components to maintain local state.

questions.text: Which Hook is commonly used for side effects such as API requests?
questions.explanation: `useEffect` is commonly used for side effects such as data fetching, subscriptions, and reacting to changes.

questions.text: Why should a frontend application avoid relying entirely on client-side validation?

options.text: Client-side validation can be bypassed, so the backend must validate data too
APIs do not accept validated data

questions.explanation: Client-side validation improves the user experience, but server-side validation is essential for security and data integrity.

questions.text: A React application needs to display products from a Node.js API. What is a typical workflow?

options.text: Store the API response in CSS
Restart the browser for every product
Send an API request, receive the data, store it in state, and render the products

questions.explanation: A frontend commonly fetches API data, stores the result in state, and renders the returned data through components.

questions.text: Why is asynchronous programming important in Node.js?

options.text: It allows I/O operations to be handled without unnecessarily blocking other work
It prevents Node.js from using APIs

questions.explanation: Asynchronous I/O helps Node.js handle many network and file operations efficiently.

questions.text: What is a Promise rejection?
questions.explanation: A Promise can be rejected when an asynchronous operation fails.

questions.text: What is rate limiting?

options.text: Restricting the number of requests a client can make within a specified period

questions.explanation: Rate limiting helps protect APIs from excessive traffic, abuse, and certain denial-of-service patterns.

questions.text: Why is centralized error handling useful in an API?

options.text: It prevents all errors from occurring
It removes the need for logging
It provides a consistent way to process and respond to application errors

questions.explanation: Centralized error handling can standardize responses and simplify application maintenance.

Source questions to address

**Question 13 — Theory**
Explain how a React frontend can communicate with a Node.js backend. What role does an API play between the two applications?

**Question 14 — Hands-on**
Create a React page that retrieves a list of students from your Node.js API and displays them. Add a form that allows a new student to be submitted to the backend.

class.title: 06. API tests, documentation and deployment
class.objectives: Explain api tests, documentation and deployment; implement the demonstrated workflow; test a normal and a failure case; justify design choices using evidence.

sections.title: Introduction and context
sections.body: A reliable API has an executable description of its expected behavior. A deployment runbook makes configuration and rollback repeatable.

sections.title: Lesson plan · 180 minutes
sections.body: 15 min: recall and goals; 45 min: guided explanation; 30 min: code demonstration; 10 min: break; 45 min: practical exercise; 20 min: review and quiz; 15 min: assignment briefing.

sections.title: Concepts and explanations
sections.body: Unit tests exercise isolated logic; integration tests exercise boundaries such as HTTP handlers and storage. Cover successful requests, invalid input and unauthorized access. Document method, path, authentication, request schema, status codes and representative responses. Configure secrets outside source control, use HTTPS at the deployment boundary and ensure logs contain request context without credentials. Test health checks, graceful shutdown and database connectivity in an isolated preview.

sections.title: Worked demonstration
sections.body:
Read the example, predict its output or behavior, then run it in the appropriate project. Framework snippets assume the lesson project and the shown imports or surrounding setup. Inspect the result before making the extension below.

// Contract example for an isolated test fixture:
const response = await fetch(`${baseUrl}/students`);
if (response.status !== 401) throw new Error('Anonymous access must be rejected');

questions.text: What is the purpose of automated testing?

options.text: To verify application behavior repeatedly and consistently

questions.explanation: Automated tests provide repeatable verification and help detect regressions.

questions.text: What is a unit test?

options.text: A test of a database server's hardware
A test of a small, isolated piece of logic
A test of the entire internet

questions.explanation: Unit tests typically focus on individual functions, modules, or units of business logic.

questions.text: What is integration testing?

options.text: Testing how multiple application components work together

questions.explanation: Integration tests verify interactions between multiple components or external dependencies.

questions.text: What is API documentation used for?

options.text: Explaining how developers can use an API

questions.explanation: API documentation describes endpoints, parameters, request formats, responses, authentication, and expected behavior.

questions.text: Which HTTP status code generally indicates that a request was successful?
questions.explanation: HTTP 200 indicates a successful request in common API scenarios.

questions.text: A developer changes an API endpoint and several frontend features stop working. What type of testing could help detect this kind of issue?
questions.explanation: Integration and end-to-end tests can verify that different parts of the system continue to work together after changes.

questions.text: What is deployment?

options.text: Making an application available in a runtime environment for users or other systems

questions.explanation: Deployment involves placing an application into an environment where it can run and be accessed.

questions.text: Why are environment variables commonly used in Node.js applications?

options.text: To manage configuration values separately from application source code

questions.explanation: Environment variables can hold values such as database URLs, API keys, ports, and other environment-specific configuration.

questions.text: Why should production secrets not be hardcoded into a Node.js application?

options.text: Hardcoded values always cause syntax errors
They can be exposed through source code or application artifacts

questions.explanation: Sensitive values should be managed securely rather than embedded directly in application source code.

questions.text: What is the purpose of a process manager such as PM2?

options.text: To help manage and keep Node.js applications running

questions.explanation: Process managers can restart applications, manage processes, and provide operational features useful for production Node.js services.
